notes: Starting point: federal AGI (IN-111 Line 1) plus net Schedule IN-112 modifications (Line 2), less the standard deduction and personal exemptions (Lines 4-7). Vermont Taxable Income is on Line 7.

Government pension of another state, and a New York State pension in particular: New York is not named anywhere in the sources and no reciprocity rule is printed. The only wording is the worksheet's 'a contributory annuity, pension, endowment, or retirement system of the U.S. government or a state government, including the Civil Service Retirement System'. public_pension_other_state is in covers of vt_other_retirement_exemption. Without that exemption (a plan that is not contributory, or earnings covered by Social Security) it stays in federal AGI with no subtraction line.

Vermont's own and federal government pensions: no general relief. Only the same worksheet wording (Vermont's as 'a state government', federal as 'the U.S. government', including the Civil Service Retirement System). Local government pensions are not named: not found in the booklet.

Private pensions, IRA distributions, employer-plan distributions and Roth conversions: no subtraction line for them on Schedule IN-112 (booklet PDF page 23, Lines 7-16) and no relief in any document. The booklet does not say in a sentence that they are taxed; they stay in federal AGI, IN-111 Line 1. The word Roth appears only in the household income instructions for the property tax and renter credits (PDF page 43). Roth conversions: not found in the booklet.

Social Security: partly exempt by election. 'You can choose to exempt your taxable social security income' (worksheet question 1). A filer over the AGI limits, or one who elects another exemption, has no other subtraction for it, and the Seniors and Retirees page speaks of benefits 'taxable in Vermont'.

Only one of the Social Security, CSRS and other-systems exemptions per return. The military exemption is outside that limit: Line 13 lets a filer electing it 'claim one additional exclusion, if eligible, enumerated by 32 V.S.A. 5830e'. Railroad Retirement (Line 14) is a separate line in full. The statute itself is not in the sources.
The IN-112 instructions and the booklet print the same retirement worksheet word for word.

Tax tables: taxable income under 75,000 uses the tables on PDF pages 47-51. All 750 printed rows, four columns each, were computed at their midpoint from the schedule rates: every row is within 2 dollars of the schedule, and the only row over 1 dollar is the first (0 to 100, printed 0). The rows are not recorded because the schedule is itself printed.

Minimum tax: when federal AGI is greater than 150,000, Line 8 is the higher of 3% of federal AGI less interest from U.S. obligations, or the schedule tax (PDF pages 11 and 46). The test is on federal AGI; the base of the 3% takes off the interest.

Additions to Vermont tax not held by any field (IN-119 Lines 1-5, booklet PDF page 11 Line 9): 24% of federal tax on qualified plans including IRA, HSA and MSA, of recapture of the federal investment tax credit, and of tax on lump-sum distributions from federal Form 4972. Self-employment income also pays the Child Care Contribution of 0.11% (IN-111 Line 21, booklet PDF page 12).

Medical Expenses Deduction (Schedule IN-112 Line 11, booklet PDF page 33): medical and dental expense from federal Schedule A Line 4, less non-allowable expenses such as retirement community fees, less IN-111 Line 6. No field holds it. Student loan interest subtraction (Line 16, not over AGI 200,000 joint or 120,000 others).

Credits on the forms not recorded as reliefs: Tax-Deductible Charitable Contribution (5% of the first 20,000, IN-111 Line 13), credit for income tax paid to another state (Schedule IN-117), Child and Dependent Care Credit (72% of federal), Child Tax Credit (1,000 per child born 2019-2025, phased down above AGI 125,000), Earned Income Tax Credit (38% of federal with a qualifying child), Veteran Tax Credit (250, phased out from AGI 25,000 to 30,000), and the IN-119 Part II business credits. Property Tax Credit and Renter Credit are separate claims on household income.

Indexing: the booklet never uses the word inflation. The only statement is on the Seniors and Retirees page, for the additional age and blind amount. That page's amount is stale for 2025 (see below), but the sentence is the only source, so it is recorded with its cite.

Civil unions follow married status (worksheet note; Schedules Y-1 and Y-2). Qualifying Widow(er) uses the joint schedule and joint standard deduction, but the retirement worksheet puts 'surviving spouse' with the 55,000 and 65,000 limits.

The separate IN-111 instructions page could not be fetched (HTTP 403); the booklet's line instructions were read in its place. Reader notes that Schedules IN-153 and IN-119 were missing are out of date: both are in the sources now and are used here.

Page conflict (the page carries no date, only 'Copyright 2026' in the footer): Social Security exemption full up to AGI 65,000 joint or 50,000 others, ending at 75,000 or 60,000. The 2025 worksheet gives 70,000 or 55,000, ending at 80,000 or 65,000. The worksheet governs.
Page conflict: CSRS and other systems limited to joint filers who 'earned $75,000 or less' and others '$60,000 or less'. The 2025 worksheet gives under 80,000 or 65,000. The worksheet governs.

Page conflict: additional deduction for age or blindness $1,000, and the filer 'must also have qualified and received the deduction at the federal level'. The 2025 booklet prints $1,250 for each standard deduction box checked on federal Form 1040. The booklet governs.

Page conflict: 'A taxpayer can only claim one' of Social Security, Military Retirement, CSRS or Other Retirement System. The 2025 Line 13 instructions let a filer using the military exemption claim one more. The booklet governs.

Page conflict: military exemption of 'the first $10,000', below 'the thresholds for the Social Security exemption'. The 2025 Line 13 and worksheet exempt all of it up to AGI 125,000, ending at 175,000. The booklet governs.

measure.as_printed: Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) on Form IN-111, Line 1 (federal Form 1040, Line 11a)

income_test.as_printed: Worksheet: full exemption if AGI is less than $70,000 (married filing jointly) or less than $55,000 (single, head of household, surviving spouse, married filing separately). Between $70,000-$80,000 and $55,000-$65,000 the exemption is multiplied by Line 8: (Line 4 minus AGI) divided by $10,000, rounded to the second decimal place, not greater than 1, where Line 4 is $80,000 (joint) or $65,000 (all other filing statuses). AGI of $80,000 or more (joint) or $65,000 or more (others): no exemption. At AGI of exactly 70,000 or 55,000 Line 8 is 1, so the printed 'less than' and the schema's 'over' give the same amount. (Line 4 - AGI) / 10,000 is the same number as 1 - (AGI - threshold) / 10,000, since Line 4 is the threshold plus 10,000: a straight-line share, width 10,000 (the printed divisor), rounded to two decimals (the worksheet's example: .481 rounds to .48).

income_test.as_printed: 'For taxpayers of any filing status with adjusted gross income equal to or less than $125,000, all military retirement and survivor benefit income is exempt.' Over $125,000 and less than $175,000: exemption = taxable military retirement income multiplied by (175,000 minus AGI) divided by $50,000, rounded to the second decimal place, not greater than 1. 'No exemption is available for taxpayers of any filing status with adjusted gross income equal to or greater than $175,000.' (175,000 - AGI) / 50,000 is the same number as 1 - (AGI - 125,000) / 50,000: a straight-line share, width 50,000 (the printed divisor), rounded to two decimals (the worksheet's example: .481 rounds to .48).
